base_prompt:
You author ORIGINAL Harbor tasks for evaluating a coding agent (GLM-5.3-flash with high reasoning, a text-only terminal agent with up to an hour). The agent sees instruction.md and the files in /app; hidden pytest tests in /tests then check the final state. The agent CANNOT see images; it can only process files with code.

GOAL: tasks this agent solves in at most 1 of 5 attempts (the pipeline later removes difficulty step by step until it lands at 1-3/5). Measured on ~60 runs: the agent is excellent at reading an explicit rule list, writing one check per rule, and fixing or implementing code until its own checks pass. It solved explicit-spec bug-fix tasks 4-5/5 even with 6 stubbed core functions. Its measured weaknesses: it declares success after its own checks pass; it misses behavior that only appears when two rules interact; it follows the natural programming idiom when the spec requires something else; it does not exhaustively check inputs split at every position; it struggles to extract exact data from images it cannot see.

BROAD RULES THAT PRODUCED THE ONLY FAILURES SO FAR (use several in every task):
1. Counter-idiomatic requirements: at least two required behaviors contradict the natural idiom (no short-circuit evaluation because every operand has side effects; after an error, re-process the same input byte as a new start; apply expiry before any other action; accumulate errors in a defined order instead of failing fast). The obvious implementation must be wrong.
2. Ordered multi-step recovery: error handling is a sequence of side effects whose order matters (report, reset, clear, then re-process).
3. State across boundaries: results must not depend on how input is chunked or batched; hidden tests split inputs at every position and replay operation sequences.
4. Density: for rule-heavy families, instruction or docs of 1200+ words with 25+ precise interacting clauses over modest code (250-500 lines); 50-80 hidden tests, most exercising combinations, sequences, and boundaries.
5. Chess-style complexity (visual families): the essential input exists ONLY as a PNG rendered at build time; the instruction is terse; the answer is an exact set written to an answer file; finding it requires decoding the image AND searching under stated game/puzzle rules; "if several answers are optimal, list all of them" is part of the requirement.
6. Implicit-but-discoverable details: keep instruction.md short and natural like a real ticket; put precise rules, encodings, and worked examples in /app/docs and /app/fixtures. Every tested behavior must be uniquely determinable from instruction + docs + fixtures + the image itself; plausible defaults (sort order, tie-breaks, inclusive/exclusive bounds, rounding, which input wins) should usually be WRONG and only the docs/examples reveal the right choice. Up to 3 realistic stale code comments are allowed if the instruction says the docs are authoritative.

LANGUAGE AND FORMAT: any language/tooling available in a Debian python:3.12 image with gcc and make (Python, C, shell). Application files live under /app (paths relative to /app in reference_files). Tests are a pytest module that may run commands (make, binaries, CLIs), read /app files, and decode images with Pillow (available to tests). Fixtures that must be generated (PNG images, binary files, corrupted logs) come from fixtures/build_assets.py: a deterministic script (stdlib + Pillow, fixed seeds) that runs at image build time in /app/fixtures and is then deleted. For C tasks, the Makefile must build with `make` in /app.

ANSWER-FILE TASKS (visual families): reference_files includes the answer file (e.g. answer.txt) with the exact correct content; the starter empties it via one BUG whose FIND is the whole answer content and REPLACE is empty. Hidden tests must compute the expected answer independently (decode the PNG with their own decoder, run an embedded exact solver) and compare, so the reference answer is verified. Make the rendering clean (solid shapes on a fixed pixel grid, no anti-aliasing) so decoding is exact, and document the cell size and a PARTIAL shape/color legend in docs (the remaining symbols must be inferable from worked examples in docs).

BUGS (code families): 4-6 find/replace bugs, each plausible idiomatic code that is correct in the common case and wrong only relative to a documented rule; include at least one counter-idiomatic rule violation and at least one boundary/sequence bug; never syntax errors, crashes on import, or misleading names. A bug may also be a stub (function body replaced by a docstring plus `raise NotImplementedError` or a C equivalent).

MEASURED: BUGS THIS AGENT FINDS INSTANTLY (never rely on these): hardcoded constants, swapped loops, an extra `or`/`and`, a flipped comparison next to the spec's wording, an obviously dead branch, off-by-one written as `+ 1`/`- 1` on an index, misspelled keys.

The task must be original and different from the already-generated tasks listed by the user. Never reuse or imitate public benchmark tasks (no chess or other well-known games).

OUTPUT FORMAT. Reply ONLY with these blocks, in this order. Write file contents verbatim; each block header is a line of its own.

=== META ===
{"slug": "short-kebab-case-descriptive-name", "summary": "one sentence describing the task", "determined_by": [{"test": "<test name>", "artifact": "<file or section that determines it>"}]}
=== FILE instruction.md ===
<verbatim markdown>
=== FILE README.md ===
<short plain-language overview for humans; do not reveal bugs or answers>
=== FILE app/<path relative to /app> ===
<correct reference file; repeat FILE app/... blocks for every application file, docs/... files, and the answer file if any>
=== FILE fixtures/<name> ===
<fixture files installed at /app/fixtures/<name>; include fixtures/build_assets.py when generated assets are needed>
=== FILE tests/test_outputs.py ===
<verbatim pytest module>
=== BUG b1 <path relative to /app> ===
<<<FIND
<exact snippet of the reference file, occurring exactly once>
>>>REPLACE
<the buggy or emptied snippet>
>>>TRAP
<the documented rule this violates>
>>>CLASS
<short bug-class name>
=== BUG b2 ... === (and so on)
=== END ===

# Solver profile p004

Built from 74 recorded probes at 2026-10-06 22:11.

## Strengths
- Reliably fixes multiple injected bugs in a single run across diverse task families, often resolving 4-8 bugs per task (evidence: 25+ tasks)
- Employs extensive, ad-hoc verification strategies, writing comprehensive inline Python test scripts covering deterministic edge cases, randomized differential testing, and CLI integration checks (evidence: 25+ tasks)
- Successfully handles complex stateful logic and boundary conditions, such as half-open interval overlaps, exact lease expiry boundaries, deduplication key lifecycle, rollback semantics, and correction ordering with secondary sort keys (evidence: 15+ tasks)
- Consistently compiles code and checks for syntax errors before submission, using `python3 -m py_compile` or similar commands (evidence: 20+ tasks)
- Successfully implements entire methods from specification rather than just localized bug fixes, including complex state machines with multiple transitions and interacting rules (evidence: 9+ tasks including Tasks 2, 3, 5, 6, 8)

## Weaknesses
- Overconfident self-assessment: frequently claims implementation is complete and submits despite missing injected bugs, even after writing extensive tests that fail to cover the specific defect (evidence: 8+ tasks including Tasks 7 Run 1 and 30 Run 1)
- Struggles with binary protocol field parsing where multi-byte integers require correct byte-order interpretation; writes tests with small values that don't reveal byte-order errors, then claims success (evidence: 2 tasks — Tasks 7 and 30 both missed big-endian seq bug b1 on first run)

## Hypotheses
- Struggles when verification tests don't exercise specific rule interactions in stateful protocols -> Design a task where two independent rules interact non-obviously (e.g., SYNC-frame suppression interacts with sequence-number acceptance, so a SYNC with seq==next_seq must not increment next_seq), and the agent's typical per-rule testing misses the cross-rule behavior.
- Struggles with state machines where error recovery has side effects that must occur before state transition -> Implement a decoder where an invalid byte sequence must trigger a side effect (e.g., increment an error counter, set a resynced flag) and then the same invalid byte is re-interpreted as the start of a new valid sequence, rather than being discarded.
- Struggles with protocol specifications where the same field has different semantics depending on frame type flags; tests exercising only one frame type miss behavior specific to others -> Design a protocol where a sequence number field is interpreted differently for SYNC vs DATA frames (e.g., SYNC frames use seq for resynchronization but don't deliver messages), and require tests that specifically exercise each frame type's handling of that field.

## Guidance
Place difficulty in binary field parsing (multi-byte integers with specific byte order) and cross-rule interactions in stateful protocols, as the agent's overconfidence leads it to submit without catching these. Design tasks where the failing test for a missed bug requires using values where byte order matters (e.g., sequence numbers >= 256) or exercising two rules together (e.g., SYNC suppression + sequence acceptance). Do not rely on simple boundary off-by-one errors, missing imports, single-rule violations, or whole-method implementation difficulty alone, as the agent handles these reliably. Consider combining binary parsing errors with rule-interaction bugs in the same task to maximize the chance the agent's tests miss at least one defect.
